verses.text: So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen.

The king said again to Esther on the second day at the banquet of wine, “What is your petition, queen Esther? It shall be granted you. What is your request? Even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.”
Then Esther the queen answered, “If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request.

For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for male and female slaves, I would have held my peace, although the adversary could not have compensated for the king’s loss.”
Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen, “Who is he, and where is he who dared presume in his heart to do so?”
Esther said, “An adversary and an enemy, even this wicked Haman!” Then Haman was afraid before the king and the queen.

The king arose in his wrath from the banquet of wine and went into the palace garden. Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen; for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king.

Then the king returned out of the palace garden into the place of the banquet of wine; and Haman had fallen on the couch where Esther was. Then the king said, “Will he even assault the queen in front of me in the house?” As the word went out of the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face.

Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs who were with the king said, “Behold, the gallows fifty cubits  high, which Haman has made for Mordecai, who spoke good for the king, is standing at Haman’s house.” The king said, “Hang him on it!”
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king’s wrath pacified.

footnotes.content: The king and Haman sit at table with Esther, yet neither knows the full weight of what's about to unfold. Sometimes I think the Lord lets injustice sit across from justice at the very same table—close enough for truth to reach it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's offer rings generous—half his kingdom!—yet Esther has learned something deeper: she knows that favor granted by earthly power is thin until it's tested. She waits for the moment when the kingdom's heart will have to choose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther speaks her petition plainly: let my life be given me. No riddles, no false humility—just the truth, spoken before a king. There's a quiet courage in asking for what matters most without pretense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We are sold…to be destroyed." The word *sold* echoes through Scripture—Joseph sold into Egypt, redemption itself called a purchase. Esther speaks the bitter truth: her people have been bartered by Haman's scheming. Yet even in captivity, she stands before a throne to reclaim what Haman presumed to take.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king asks *who*—who dared? He hasn't grasped it yet, but his question opens the door. Sometimes the Lord works through simple questions, drawing out the truth that was always waiting to be named.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "This wicked Haman." Four words, and the man who thought himself untouchable learns he was known all along. Esther names him plainly, and the room shifts. Fear, that strange master, now grips the wrong man.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman's hope dies in an instant—he sees it in the king's wrath, in the garden where the king walks to cool his anger. The man who plotted another's death now finds death plotting his own end. Mercy often feels this way to those who've shown none.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman falls on Esther's couch in desperation—the very gesture seals his doom. The king sees it as assault on the queen, the unthinkable transgression. Sometimes our own panic does what our accusers couldn't: it speaks against us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The gallows stand fifty cubits high—Haman's monument to his own pride, built to hang Mordecai. Harbonah's simple report names them and, in naming, condemns their builder. The instrument of revenge often becomes the measure of justice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman hanged on his own gallows—readers today hear an echo in how the Lord turns the plots of the prideful back upon their own heads. We've seen it a thousand times since: the snare set for the innocent catches the setter instead. Grace doesn't always intervene loudly; sometimes it simply lets justice follow its course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
